prompt: Use case: illustration-story. Asset type: a production atlas of circular illustrated tokens for Creation, an original elemental myth about making a vast living world. The reference is the APPROVED STYLE AND CONTINUITY anchor, not a sheet to copy unchanged. Paint new subjects in exactly that family: luminous opaque gouache, selective fine ink contours, strong simplified silhouettes readable at 64px; deep lapis interiors, jade and turquoise, burnt ochre, muted coral, warm ivory light, very narrow ivory-gold rims. Not glossy coins or flat generic pictograms. Each icon is a complete perfect CIRCLE with opaque painted interior and transparent empty space outside. Center each circle in its own equal grid cell, circle diameter 80 percent of the shorter cell side, generous empty gutters. Absolutely no letters, names, numbers, grid lines, labels, UI, watermark or cast shadows outside circles. No modern laboratory hardware, books, houses or buildings. Only the specified object inside each circle, with a simple dark ground or essential local context. Tiny details must not carry the meaning. Related states should differ in structure, not merely colour. Follow item order exactly, left to right, top to bottom. Exactly 20 circles in 5 columns and 4 rows. Landscape atlas. Exact cell subjects: CELL 1, Volcano: A steep dark volcanic cone releases a compact coral eruption and a short glowing lava stream down one flank, with an exposed crater at the summit. Distinguish: Land cone and crater dominate, without surrounding ocean horizon, seafloor vent plume or incoming body. CELL 2, Hydrothermal vent: Two rough dark mineral chimneys rise from the deep seafloor, releasing thick black plumes into jade water; small pale mineral edges catch the faint light. Distinguish: Underwater chimneys with dark plumes, not an erupting cone, trench or diagram of microscopic chemistry. CELL 3, Weathered rock: A large ochre rock is split by water-darkened cracks, with rounded corners, detached chips and a short rivulet carrying fine grains away from its base. Distinguish: Visible rock breaking down and material leaving it; no organic roots or already settled sediment fan. CELL 4, Mineral-rich sea: At a rocky coast, a jade river plume fans into blue sea carrying a few bright mineral grains that grow smaller and fade into the water. Show the moving water and mineral source together. Distinguish: Dissolving material enters a coastal water plume; no pile of crystals, laboratory vessel or claim that dissolved ions remain visible. CELL 5, Volcanic island: A bare dark volcanic island rises from a broad blue sea, with a small ochre crater and fresh black lava slopes reaching directly into the water. Distinguish: Isolated ocean-surrounded cone with no plants or animals; eruption is secondary to new island shape. CELL 6, Organic molecules: Several irregular chains and small loops of joined ochre, ivory and coral grains drift in dark jade water beside one mineral surface. Use a hand-painted microscopic atlas convention, without letters, bonds as technical diagrams or equipment. Distinguish: Loose varied connected chains, not dense nuclear clusters, sun-energized compact packets or enclosing membranes. CELL 7, Membranes: Two thin translucent jade bubbles float in dark water, each with a clear double-edged boundary enclosing nearly empty fluid; one open curved sheet is folding toward closure. Distinguish: Simple empty flexible boundaries without internal living structures, division or hard shell ridges. CELL 8, Chemical fuel: A small cluster of tightly joined coral and ochre molecular grains catches a narrow shaft of sunlight, with warm light retained in the cluster after the beam passes. Keep a few unlit grains nearby for contrast. Distinguish: A molecular energy-storage convention, with no flame, battery, fuel can or suggestion of food being oxygen. CELL 9, Variation: Four related jade cells form a loose branching family, sharing the same basic boundary but differing slightly in size and in the arrangement of their coral internal threads. Distinguish: Small inherited differences among related cells, without a division waist or animal coat differences. CELL 10, Sun-fed cells: Three jade-green cells lie close beneath a warm shaft of sunlight, their interiors filled with small leaf-green granules; a few pale bubbles leave the group. Distinguish: Sunlit microbial group with green granules, not a leafy sea plant or a cell taking oxygen inward. CELL 11, Microbial mats: A low emerald and ochre living film coats a flat wet rock, shown with one cut edge revealing several thin soft layers; tiny bubbles sit along its surface. Distinguish: Flat microbial carpet rather than domed stone structures, leafy moss or a protected underside close-up. CELL 12, Stromatolites: Three rounded low domes rise in shallow water, their cutaway sides revealing closely stacked wavy ochre and jade laminae beneath a thin living green surface. Distinguish: Built domed laminated structures, not flat mats, straight iron bands or branching animal skeletons. CELL 13, Oxygen: Several pale paired spheres rise as bubbles from a small green microbial patch in water, with one pair enlarged near the foreground. The repeated pair is a simple atlas convention for oxygen. Distinguish: Paired gas motif arising from living water; ozone uses triads high around a planet and sky shows accumulated atmosphere. CELL 14, Rusted seabed: A shallow seabed is stained with broad coral-red and dark ochre deposits, with a thin greenish water layer and a few settling pale particles above it. Distinguish: Loose rust-colored deposits under water, without hardened repeating stripes or prepared pigment puddles. CELL 15, Banded iron: A broken upright slab exposes bold alternating dark iron-grey and coral-red horizontal bands, with a rough outer edge and a small wet seabed base. Distinguish: Repeated hard contrasting mineral stripes, without loose mud, one black carbon seam or shell impressions. CELL 16, Oxygen-rich sky: The familiar hooked continent curves beneath a broad clear pale-blue atmospheric band, containing a few paired ivory gas marks well above the sea. Distinguish: Broad lower atmosphere around the world; ozone is a separate thin high cap and oxygen alone is bubbles above microbes. CELL 17, Ozone layer: A thin luminous jade shell lies high above the familiar curved planet, with three-part pale gas clusters and several short incoming violet light rays fading at the shell. Distinguish: Thin high atmospheric shield absorbing rays; no broad low gas band, symmetric magnetic loops or polar curtains. CELL 18, Oxygen-using cells: One pale jade cell draws paired ivory gas marks inward beside a separate small ochre food grain; its simple interior shows a warm coral glow. Distinguish: Oxygen and a separate food particle enter the cell, without sunlight or a distinct engulfed partner. CELL 19, Sheltered microbes: A lifted corner of a thick green microbial mat reveals a dark sealed pocket in the underlying mud, containing several tiny pale cells protected beneath the living surface. Distinguish: Microbes beneath an oxygen-excluding mud-and-mat roof, not exposed surface growth, wood shelter or free bubbles. CELL 20, Cell colonies: A loose rosette of eight visibly separate jade cells touches edge to edge, each cell retaining its own outline and simple interior. Distinguish: Many similar cells loosely joined, without a differentiated continuous body or a host enclosing a partner. Keep the common circle size and painted finish. Anatomical lineages matter: insects have six legs, birds feathered wings, bats membranous finger-supported wings. A depicted early cell is a symbolic magnified view, not a modern laboratory slide. The world is not Earth's recognizable map. People, if listed, have varied warm earth-brown complexions, simplified features and no modern objects. Never add people, plants or animals to a subject that predates them. Do not draw the subject names.
